obs: "Read as this should be read on the natural understanding of the phrasing"; "confirms and emphasizes the plain intendment of the language."
Employees of Department of Public Health v. Department of Public Health
"The history and tradition of the Eleventh Amendment indicate that by reason of that barrier a federal court is not competent to render judgment against a nonconsenting State."
"the necessary predicate for that doctrine was congres[s]ional intent to abrogate the immunity conferred by the Eleventh Amendment."
"The provisions of the Social Security Act relied upon by plaintiffs were held by their terms not to authorize suit against anyone"

“I find neither ground a persuasive justification for dilution of the clear statement rule… counsel-fee awards cannot be viewed as having the kind of ancillary effect on the state treasury… that avoids the need for an explicit waiver of Eleventh Amendment protections… Because explicit authorization to join a State as defendant… is absent here…”
"But in this sensitive area of conflicting interests of constitutional dimension, we should not permit items of legislative history to substitute for explicit statutory language."
"Congress may override this immunity when it acts pursuant to the power granted it under 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment, but it must make its intent to do so unmistakably clear."
Will v. Michigan Department of State Police
“But in deciphering congressional intent as to the scope of 1983, the scope of the Eleventh Amendment is a consideration, and we decline to adopt a reading of 1983 that disregards it.”
Missouri v. Jenkins Ex Rel. Agyei
"subsequent decisions of this Court that require Congress to express its intention to abrogate the Eleventh Amendment in unmistakable language in the statute itself."
Hoffman v. Connecticut Department of Income Maintenance
"Nothing in 106(c) provides a similar express authorization for monetary recovery from the States."
“States are not persons within the meaning of 1983 because Congress presumably would not have abrogated state sovereign immunity without a clear statement of its intent to do so”
Equal Employment Opportunity Commission v. Arabian American Oil Co.

“If this logic is sufficiently sharp to pierce the dense armor afforded the States by the clear-statement abrogation rule of Atascadero State Hospital v. Scanlon, 473 U. S., at 242-243; accord, Dellmuth v. Muth, 491 U. S., at 230”
Blatchford v. Native Village of Noatak

"our cases require Congress exercise of the power to abrogate state sovereign immunity, where it exists, to be exercised with unmistakeable clarity." ... "We have repeatedly said that this power to abrogate can only be exercised by a clear legislative statement." ... "Congress may abrogate the States constitutionally secured immunity from suit in federal court only by making its intention unmistakably clear in the language of the statute."
Blatchford v. Native Village of Noatak

“It is premised on the perception that Congress does not casually alter the balance of power between the Federal Government and the States… this Court has erected the clear-statement rule in order to be certain that abrogation is Congress plan.”
Blatchford v. Native Village of Noatak
"The fact that Congress grants jurisdiction to hear a claim does not suffice to show Congress has abrogated all defenses to that claim. The issues are wholly distinct."
Barnes v. E-Systems, Inc. Group Hospital Medical & Surgical Ins. Plan
"But ERISA makes no mention of monetary relief, and in any event our cases do not favor implicit abrogation of Eleventh Amendment immunity."
"(to subject States to suits for money damages, Congress need only make that intent clear, and need not refer explicitly to the Eleventh Amendment)"
Florida Prepaid Postsecondary Education Expense Board v. College Savings Bank

"To determine the merits of this proposition, we must answer two questions: first, whether Congress has unequivocally expresse[d] its intent to abrogate the immunity, . . ."; "Congress has made its intention to abrogate the States immunity unmistakably clear in the language of the statute."
"As we later recognized, however, even this statute did not clearly create a cause of action against the States."
Nevada Department of Human Resources v. William Hibbs
"Congress may, however, abrogate such immunity in federal court if it makes its intention to abrogate unmistakably clear in the language of the statute"
Nevada Department of Human Resources v. Hibbs
"The clarity of Congress intent here is not fairly debatable."
Central Virginia Community College v. Katz
"Congress had failed to make sufficiently clear its intent to abrogate state sovereign immunity"
"As with all waivers of sovereign immunity, the question is whether the State has unequivocally consented to suit in federal court."
Coleman v. Court of Appeals of Maryland
"Congress must mak[e] its intention to abrogate unmistakably clear in the language of the statute."
Torres v. Texas Department of Public Safety
“To be clear, I am not disputing whether USERRA speaks clearly enough to express a congressional intent to abrogate the States’ sovereign immunity in their own courts”
"courts have consistently held that nothing but express words, or an insur-mountable implication would justify the conclusion that lawmakers intended to abrogate the States’ sovereign immunity."
Financial Oversight and Management Bd. for P. R. v. Centro De Periodismo Investigativo, Inc.
"Under long-settled law, Congress must use unmistakable language to abrogate sovereign immunity. Nothing in the statute creating the board meets that high bar."
Lac du Flambeau Band of Lake Superior Chippewa Indians v. Coughlin

“But, as explained at the outset, supra, at 4, the clear-statement rule is not a magic-words requirement. Thus, Congress did not have to include a specific reference to federally recognized tribes in order to make clear that it intended for tribes to be covered by the abrogation provision. As long as Congress speaks unequivocally, it passes the clear-statement test”
“(So the doctrine would function like the rule that Congress must speak clearly toabrogate state sovereign immunity.)”
